anna: Heads up — noticed a big drop in prefix cache hit rate after the kernel-select rollout last night. overall hit went 82% -> 59% on prod cohort A. tail p99 latency for gen requests up ~23%.
devin: ack. can you paste the perf dump and sample keys? :eyes:
anna: quick summary from profiler: \n```
- kernel-select v2 deploy @ 03:12 UTC
- avg seq len shifted +6 tokens for hot prompts
- cache hit rate (prefix): 82% -> 59%
- warmup miss rate spiked, kv eviction rate +18%
- CPU time for batching logic +12ms per request
```
I also sampled ~200 missed keys and noticed tiny whitespace/arg-order diffs and a few requests had tokenizer_version null.
kevin: hmm tokenizer_version null is a red flag — we started defaulting to tokenizer v3 in the runtime image but didn't pin the value into the probe metadata. that can fragment keys across versions.
sarah: also saw a subset where tool call arg ordering changed (we log tools as JSON but not canonicalized). sometimes `tool_args` arrives as `[a,b]` vs `[b,a]` depending on frontend ordering. those become distinct cache keys.
devin: that explains fragmentation. kernel-select bump changed batching heuristics which increased small-prefix throughput and exposed more of these borderline keys (they used to be batched/merged differently). so we see both distribution and keying causes.
anna: proposal: 1) include `tokenizer_version` and `model_variant` as explicit fields in cache key (string). 2) add a canonicalizer that sorts tool arg keys and removes insignificant whitespace in prompt/systems. 3) backfill warmup for the last 48h of hot prefixes for the affected cohort.
kevin: +1 on tokenizer_version in key. canonicalizer needs to be deterministic and cheap. avoid heavyweight normalizations that change semantics (e.g., we shouldn't strip newlines inside code blocks).
sarah: agree. canonicalization rules I'd use: trim trailing/leading whitespace on each line, normalize CRLF -> LF, collapse multiple spaces outside fenced code to single space, and for tool args: sort object keys and sort arrays of primitive args but preserve arrays of objects order (too risky to reorder complex structs).
devin: to test cheaply, we can run an A/B where A uses new keying and canonicalizer but writes misses to a new cache namespace (so we don't poison current cache), then run a warmup script that replays top prefixes into that namespace. sample warmup script (python):\n```
# warmup replay (very small example)
import requests
for p in top_prefixes[:2000]:
    requests.post('https://self-hosted.warmup.local/replay', json={'prefix': p, 'model': 'rwd-13b-v1'})
```
we'll measure hit-rate on the new namespace before flipping.
anna: nice. estimated warming cost for 2k prefixes is ~4 GPU-hours for the cohort, under our burst budget.
kevin: consider also adding a short-lived `canonicalization_version` tag in key so we can roll-forward/back safely.
anna: good call. infra-bot can you create a canary job: create new cache namespace `prefx-v2-test-<date>`, enable tokenizer_version & canonicalization_version in key, run warmup script for cohort A for 24h, collect hit-rate + p99 latency, and then post results?
infra-bot: Received. scheduled job prefex-v2-test-2026-03-18. resources: 1x g4dn, 4h warmup window, telemetry hooks enabled. I'll post status in this thread once warmup completes. (reacts :white_check_mark:)
devin: once warmup is done we'll compare: current namespace hit-rate vs test namespace. if test >= pre-rollout baseline (80%+) and p99 improves, we can flip.
sarah: small note: also audit client SDKs for inconsistent tool arg serialization. I can run a quick grep across web + mobile codepaths for JSON.stringify order usage.
kevin: I'll prepare a lightweight canonicalizer PR (rust) and opt it into runtime via feature flag. keep rollout gated.
anna: thanks team. action items summarized: \n- kevin: PR canonicalizer + key change (include tokenizer_version & canonicalization_version)
- sarah: audit SDKs for serialization inconsistencies
- devin: run canary warmup and collect metrics
- infra-bot: run scheduled warmup job and report
I'll follow up with the missed-key samples in a gist.
